extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, law, and government (those studying the origins and justification of civil society and authority)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains the philosophical standards for domestic authority, the nature and ends of marriage and family, the distinction between household and political power, and the social-contract rules that create civil society (consent, majority rule, purpose of government).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ends of marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: For all the ends of marriage being to be obtained under politic government, as well as in the state of nature... viz. procreation and mutual support and assistance whilst they are together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marriage's chief ends are procreation and the mutual support/assistance of spouses while together. Locke explains the biological and social reasons for longer conjugal bonds (female pregnancy and prolonged child dependency) and that conjugal society is justified insofar as it secures procreation, education of children until they can provide for themselves, and mutual maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conjugal bonds may be determinable
rubrics_metrics.description: This compact, where procreation and education are secured, and inheritance taken care for, may not be made determinable, either by consent, or at a certain time, or upon certain conditions, as well as any other voluntary compacts...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke raises that marriage need not necessarily be perpetual by nature; where no positive law makes contracts perpetual, spouses could agree (by consent or condition) to make the conjugal compact determinable. This is a normative point: marriage's duration can be set by agreement if it does not frustrate its ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of husband’s authority within marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: The last determination... naturally falls to the man's share, as the abler and the stronger. But this reaching but to the things of their common interest and property, leaves the wife in the full and free possession of what by contract is her peculiar right, and gives the husband no more power over her life than she has over his.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Husband's prerogative is limited to joint concerns and property necessary to the ends of marriage; it is not an absolute monarchical authority. The wife retains her peculiar rights and may have liberty to separate where natural right or contract allows. Civil magistrate only decides controversies, not to abridge natural rights necessary for marriage's ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between master-and-servant and slavery
rubrics_metrics.description: A freeman makes himself a servant to another, by selling him, for a certain time, the service he undertakes to do, in exchange for wages... But there is another sort of servants... slaves, who being captives taken in a just war, are by the right of nature subjected to the absolute dominion and arbitrary power of their masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contractual service (servant) is temporary and limited by the contract and family discipline; slavery (captives from just war) is treated as forfeiture of life/liberty/property and yields absolute dominion. This distinction justifies different legal/moral treatment of servitude vs slavery in Locke's framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: The household (paterfamilias) is not a political commonwealth
rubrics_metrics.description: The master of a family with wife, children, servants, and slaves... what resemblance soever it may have... yet is very far from it, both in its constitution, power and end: or if it must be thought a monarchy, and the paterfamilias the absolute monarch in it, absolute monarchy will have but a very shattered and short power...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a household may look like a little commonwealth, the master lacks legislative authority, broad sovereign powers, and his power is limited in time and extent over individuals (except slaves). Therefore a family does not constitute political society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of political (civil) society
rubrics_metrics.description: Political society... is where every one of the members hath quitted this natural power, resigned it up into the hands of the community in all cases that exclude him not from appealing for protection to the law established by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil society begins where individuals give up the natural, private right to judge and punish, and instead place that power in a common authority (laws and judicature) to decide differences and punish offences. Key elements: resignation of private execution, establishment of standing laws and impartial judges, and a right of appeal to a public authority rather than private vengeance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements for a political society (standing rules, common judge, execution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The community comes to be umpire, by settled standing rules, indifferent, and the same to all parties; and by men having authority from the community, for the execution of those rules, decides all the differences... and punishes those offences which any member hath committed against the society, with such penalties as the law has established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A lawful commonwealth must provide known laws (standing rules), an impartial judicature to apply them uniformly, and authorized officers to execute the laws and punish offences. These institutions distinguish civil society from the state of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary end of civil society: preservation of property
rubrics_metrics.description: All this for the preservation of the property of all the members of that society, as far as is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke frames preservation of property (life, liberty, estate) as the chief end of civil government. Law-making, punishment, and war/peace powers are instruments directed to that end and must be justified by it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Members' duty to assist execution of judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: With the judgment of offences, which he has given up to the legislative... he has given a right to the commonwealth to employ his force, for the execution of the judgments of the commonwealth, whenever he shall be called to it; which indeed are his own judgments, they being made by himself, or his representative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By joining a political society individuals authorize the community to execute its judgments and may owe their assistance (e.g., enforce sentences or join defense) to the commonwealth when required, because the laws represent their collective will.

rubrics_metrics.name: Majority rule binds individuals in a political community
rubrics_metrics.description: When any number of men have, by the consent of every individual, made a community, they are thereby made that community one body, with a power to act as one body, which is only by the will and determination of the majority... every man... puts himself under an obligation... to submit to the determination of the majority, and to be concluded by it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a collective body to function and act as one, the will of the majority must determine the community's actions. Consent to majority decision is treated as implicit in the compact of forming a commonwealth; absent such acceptance the community could not effectively act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consent required to be subjected to political power
rubrics_metrics.description: No one can be put out of this estate, and subjected to the political power of another, without his own consent. The only way whereby any one divests himself of his natural liberty... is by agreeing with other men to join and unite into a community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate political authority requires the consent of the governed: one cannot be lawfully subjected to political power without having agreed to enter civil society. This is a foundational social-contract requirement in Locke's account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute monarchy inconsistent with civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: Absolute monarchy... is indeed inconsistent with civil society, and so can be no form of civil-government at all: for the end of civil society, being to avoid... every man’s being judge in his own case, by setting up a known authority, to which every one of that society may appeal...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a single person holds all legislative and executive authority with no impartial judge or appeal, subjects are left without the protections civil society provides and are effectively in the state of nature relative to the prince. Hence absolute sovereignty concentrated in one person contradicts the purpose of civil society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for collective legislature to secure property and equal law
rubrics_metrics.description: The people finding their properties not secure under the government... could never be safe nor at rest, nor think themselves in civil society, till the legislature was placed in collective bodies of men... By which means every single person became subject, equally with other the meanest men, to those laws, which he himself, as part of the legislative, had established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Placing legislative power in collective bodies (senate, parliament, etc.) prevents arbitrary rule and ensures laws are public and apply equally. Collective legislatures make laws that represent the consent of many, giving each person a share in law-making and protection of property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical forms of government may start from paternal or military authority but derive legitimacy from consent
rubrics_metrics.description: If we look back... we shall generally find them under the government and administration of one man... the father having... the same power with every man else to punish... was fittest to be trusted... And where several families met, and consented to continue together... they used their natural freedom, to set up him, whom they judged the ablest, and most likely, to rule well over them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke acknowledges historical emergence of single-person rule (paternal authority, wartime generals) but insists such arrangements often originated or were sustained by the consent of the people. Even when government appears monarchical, its legitimacy in his account rests on the original consent and agreement of the governed.
